units.title: Reading Cursive
units.blurb: Reading cursive letters, words and notes, and the handwriting of old documents.

topics.title: Sitting to Write
topics.short: Sit tall and back in the chair, feet flat on the floor, with both arms resting on the table.
topics.trouble: Children curl up, kneel on the chair or lean far over the paper. Sitting tall with both arms on the table gives the writing hand room to move.

topics.title: Holding the Pencil
topics.short: Hold the pencil with the thumb and pointer finger, let it rest on the middle finger, a little way up from the point, and hold it lightly.
topics.trouble: Children wrap the whole hand around the pencil, pinch it right at the point, or squeeze hard. The usual grip most teachers show is the three-finger hold; some writers who use four fingers also write well.

topics.title: Placing the Paper
topics.short: Keep the paper in front of you and hold it still with your other hand. For cursive, tilt it: top to the left for a right hand, top to the right for a left hand.
topics.trouble: Children let the paper slide around, or a left-handed writer copies the tilt a right-handed neighbor uses.

topics.title: The Lines We Write On
topics.short: Letters sit on the baseline. Short letters reach the middle line, tall letters reach the top line, and tail letters go below the baseline.
topics.trouble: Children let letters float above the baseline, or make every letter the same height.

topics.title: The Strokes That Make Letters
topics.short: Every print letter is made of a few strokes: lines down, lines across, slants and circles. Each stroke has a start and a direction.
topics.trouble: Children draw letters like pictures, starting anywhere and going any way, which makes writing slow and letters uneven.

topics.title: Start at the Top
topics.short: Most strokes start at the top and go down. Tall letters like b, h, k, l and t start at the top line; short letters start at the middle line.
topics.trouble: Children start lines at the bottom and push up, or start a tall letter at the middle line.

topics.title: Stick Letters: l, i and t
topics.short: l, i and t are made of straight lines: down from the top, then a dot or a cross.
topics.trouble: Children make i as tall as l, or cross t at the top instead of at the middle line.

topics.title: Circle Letters: c, o, a, d, g and q
topics.short: Start just below the middle line and curve back around, the way c begins. a, d, g and q add a line down.
topics.trouble: Children draw the circle clockwise, starting at the bottom, so the circle and its line don’t meet neatly.

topics.title: Down, Up and Over: r, n, m, h, b and p
topics.short: Pull down, then go back up the line and over the hump: r, n, m and h. b and p add a round bump.
topics.trouble: Children start the hump away from the line, so it doesn’t touch, or make the humps of m different sizes.

topics.title: Slant Letters: v, w, x, y, z and k
topics.short: These letters use slanted lines: down to the right, down to the left, or both.
topics.trouble: Children make the two sides of v and w uneven, or start y’s long slant at the wrong side.

topics.title: Special Letters: e, f, j, s and u
topics.short: e starts across the middle; f starts with a hook near the top; j has a tail and a dot; s curves back and forth; u goes down, around and up.
topics.trouble: Children start e at the top like c, or make s backward.

topics.title: Tall, Short and Tail Letters
topics.short: Tall letters (b d f h k l t) reach the top line, short letters stay below the middle line, and tail letters (g j p q y) go down below the baseline.
topics.trouble: Children make tails sit on the baseline (g and y look like a and v), or make tall and short letters the same size.

topics.title: Capitals with Straight Lines
topics.short: E, F, H, I, L and T are made of lines down and across. Every capital starts at the top line and reaches the baseline.
topics.trouble: Children make the middle bar of E and F too high or too low, or draw the lines in a different order each time.

topics.title: Capitals with Slants
topics.short: A, K, M, N, V, W, X, Y and Z use slanted lines from the top line to the baseline.
topics.trouble: Children make N or Z backward, or make the middle of M stop halfway.

topics.title: Capitals with Curves
topics.short: B, C, D, G, J, O, P, Q, R, S and U use curves; B, D, P and R start with a line down.
topics.trouble: Children make the bumps of B the same size as one big bump (like D), or start the curve of C at the bottom.

topics.title: b, d, p and q
topics.short: b starts with a tall line and then the bump; d starts with a c and then the tall line. p and q go below the baseline.
topics.trouble: Children mix up b and d, and p and q, which are mirror images. Remember: d begins with c, and c comes before d in the alphabet.

topics.title: Letters Close Together
topics.short: Letters in a word sit close, but not touching.
topics.trouble: Children leave big gaps inside a word, so it looks like two words.

topics.title: A Finger Space Between Words
topics.short: Leave about one finger’s width between words.
topics.trouble: Children run words together, or leave no space after a period.

topics.title: Sitting on the Lines
topics.short: Every letter sits on the baseline and stays the right size for its kind.
topics.trouble: Children let letters drift above the baseline at the end of a line, or grow bigger as they go.

topics.title: Copying Neatly
topics.short: Copy a sentence letter by letter: check the spaces, the sizes, the capital at the start and the mark at the end.
topics.trouble: Children copy quickly and skip a word or a letter; reading the copy back against the model catches it.

topics.title: Writing 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4
topics.short: Write each number from the top: 0 curves around, 1 goes straight down, 2 and 3 curve, 4 goes down, across, then down.
topics.trouble: Children start 0 at the bottom, or write 3 and 4 backward.

topics.title: Writing 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9
topics.short: 5 goes down and around, then gets its hat; 6 curves down into a loop; 7 goes across, then slants down; 8 is an S that comes back up; 9 is a circle and a line.
topics.trouble: Children put the hat on 5 first and lose their place, or start 8 with two circles stacked up.

topics.title: Numbers That Get Flipped
topics.short: 2, 3, 5, 7 and 9 face a certain way. Check each one: 3 and 5 curve to the right; 9 has its circle on the left.
topics.trouble: Children write 3, 5, 7 and 9 backward, which is common at first and fades with practice.

topics.title: What Cursive Is
topics.short: In cursive the letters of a word are joined, so the pencil stays down. People use it to write quickly, to sign their names, and to read old letters and documents.
topics.trouble: Children think cursive is a different alphabet. It has the same 26 letters, with joining strokes and some new shapes.

topics.title: The Basic Cursive Strokes
topics.short: Most cursive letters are built from an undercurve (a swing up like a smile), an overcurve (a hill), a downcurve (like the start of c) and a slant line.
topics.trouble: Children make the curves into straight lines, which makes the letters hard to join smoothly.

topics.title: The Cursive Slant
topics.short: All cursive letters lean the same way, like rain blowing in the wind.
topics.trouble: Children let some letters lean and others stand up straight or lean backward. Tilting the paper helps.

topics.title: Cursive i, t, u and w
topics.short: These letters start with an undercurve, slant down and swing up. Dot i and cross t after you finish the word.
topics.trouble: Children dot i and cross t before the word is done, breaking the flow, or make t as tall as l.

topics.title: Loop Letters: e, l, h, k, b and f
topics.short: Swing up into a loop: small for e, tall for l, h, k, b and f. f also has a loop below the baseline.
topics.trouble: Children make the loops too fat, too thin (closed), or the wrong height, so l looks like e.

topics.title: The c Family: a, c, d, g, o and q
topics.short: Swing up, curve back around like c, and close the letter at the top. d goes up tall; g and q go below.
topics.trouble: Children leave the tops of a, d, g and o open, so a looks like u and d like cl.

topics.title: Hill Letters: n, m, v, x, y and z
topics.short: Start with an overcurve, a hill, then slant down. m has three hills’ worth of strokes, n two.
topics.trouble: Children make the hills pointed like v, so n looks like u and m like w.

topics.title: Cursive r, s, p and j
topics.short: r and s go up to a point a little above the middle line; p and j go down below the baseline.
topics.trouble: Children make cursive r and s look like their print forms, which won’t join, or make r’s shoulder too long so it looks like n.

topics.title: Tricky Connectors: b, o, v and w
topics.short: b, o, v and w end up at the middle line, not on the baseline, so the next letter joins with a little bridge along the top.
topics.trouble: Children drop down to the baseline after o or w, so on looks like an and we looks like ue.

topics.title: Cursive Capitals A, C, E and O
topics.short: These capitals start near the top with a curve around to the left.
topics.trouble: Children write a print capital in a cursive word, or make the cursive capital no taller than a small letter.

topics.title: Cursive Capitals H, K, M, N, U, V, W, X, Y and Z
topics.short: Many of these start with a small hook and a hill at the top, then slant down.
topics.trouble: Children make M and N without the starting hook, or mix up cursive U and V.

topics.title: Cursive Capitals B, F, P, R and T
topics.short: Start with a slant down, then come back up for the bumps of B, P and R; F and T start with a wavy top.
topics.trouble: Children forget the top of F and T, or confuse cursive F with T (F has a cross in the middle).

topics.title: Cursive Capitals D, G, I, J, L, Q and S
topics.short: These capitals have shapes of their own: I and J start with a swing up from the middle; L and S loop; cursive Q looks like a 2.
topics.trouble: Children don’t recognize cursive G, Q, I and J when reading, because they look little like print.

topics.title: Joining Letters
topics.short: Each letter ends with an exit stroke that becomes the next letter’s entry stroke, so the pencil stays down through the word.
topics.trouble: Children lift the pencil after every letter, so the word comes out as separate pieces.

topics.title: Capitals That Join and Capitals That Don’t
topics.short: Some cursive capitals join the next letter (A, C, E, H, K, M, N, U and others); some usually stand alone (B, D, O, P, S, V, W and others).
topics.trouble: Children force a join after a capital that ends high or on the left. Writers and books differ on a few capitals; either way is fine if it is clear.

topics.title: Spacing Joined Words
topics.short: End a word with its exit stroke, lift the pencil, and start the next word about one small o’s width away.
topics.trouble: Children join the last letter of one word to the first of the next, so two words read as one.

topics.title: Writing Sentences in Cursive
topics.short: Start with a cursive capital, join the letters of each word, space the words, and end with a mark.
topics.trouble: Children speed up and the letters lose their shapes; steady and readable comes before fast.

topics.title: Checking Letter Shapes
topics.short: Look for closed tops (a, d, g, o), clear loops (e, l), round hills (n, m) and even slant.
topics.trouble: Children check spelling but not shapes, so a word like clear reads as dear.

topics.title: Signing Your Name
topics.short: A signature is your name in your own handwriting, usually in cursive. Write it the same way each time and keep it readable.
topics.trouble: Children think a signature must be fancy or unreadable. A clear, steady signature is a good one.

topics.title: Reading Cursive Letters
topics.short: Match each cursive letter to its print letter, especially the ones that look different: cursive r, s, z, G, I, J and Q.
topics.trouble: Children who can write cursive still stall when reading it, because some capitals look little like print.

topics.title: Reading Cursive Words
topics.short: Read a cursive word letter by letter at first, then as a whole.
topics.trouble: Children guess from the first letter; checking each letter, especially the joins after b, o, v and w, prevents mistakes.

topics.title: Reading Old Handwriting
topics.short: Old letters and documents use cursive styles of their time, sometimes with the long s (ſ), which looks much like f but has no crossbar, or only a nub on the left.
topics.trouble: Children read the long s as f (Congreſs as Congrefs). The long s was an ordinary lowercase s in older writing.
